pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Protecting Endangered Animals (ages 9–11): the strategies people use to save endangered species — protected areas (national parks, marine reserves), captive breeding and reintroduction, anti-poaching patrols, wildlife corridors linking habitats, and laws banning trade — and that individuals, including children, can help through habitat-friendly choices.
• Standards — UK (DfE): applies Y4/Y6 ecology and human-impact aims to solutions; supports the working-scientifically and science-in-society strands (evaluating evidence for what works).
• Standards — US (NGSS): 3-LS4-4 (claim about a solution to a problem caused by environmental change); MS-LS2-5 ([curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-LS2-5]).
• Operational details: cover ≥3 strategies with real success stories — captive breeding + reintroduction (California condor, Arabian oryx back from near-extinction), protected areas/reserves, anti-poaching patrols (rhino, elephant), wildlife corridors (reconnecting fragmented habitat), and trade bans (CITES ivory ban). Stress that conservation must protect BOTH habitats AND individual species — saving an animal without its habitat fails. Include concrete child/family actions (habitat-friendly gardens, sustainable choices, supporting conservation). Frame as matching the RIGHT strategy to the specific threat.
• Checkpoint — A (concrete, ~9): name at least one conservation strategy and an animal it helped. B (transitional, ~10): describe 3 strategies with examples and one action a child can take. C (formal, ~11): match a strategy to the threat it addresses and explain why protecting habitat AND species together matters.
bestPractices: Teach conservation as matching strategy to threat (poaching → patrols/trade bans; habitat fragmentation → corridors; tiny population → captive breeding) so pupils reason about fit, not just list actions.
Use documented success stories (condor, oryx) to show conservation can work, building agency rather than despair.
Make the habitat-AND-species point explicit with a counter-case: breeding animals with nowhere to release them fails — both are needed.
Include realistic, specific child/family actions tied to habitat so 'you can help' is concrete, not a platitude.
keyRepresentations: A threat→strategy matching board (poaching, habitat loss, small population, isolation → the fitting intervention).
A recovery graph showing a species (condor/oryx) climbing back from near-zero after intervention.
A fragmented-habitat map with a wildlife corridor reconnecting patches.
A 'both needed' pairing: protected species + protected habitat = success.
commonMisconceptions: 'Just put endangered animals in zoos and they're saved' — captive breeding only works with habitat to release them back into; zoos alone aren't a solution.
'One strategy fixes every species' — different threats need different, matched interventions.
'Conservation never works / it's hopeless' — documented recoveries (condor, oryx) show it can succeed.
'Only scientists and governments can help' — individual and family choices affect habitats too.
'Protecting the animal is enough without protecting its habitat' — a species can't survive without the habitat it depends on.

learn.summary: Learners aged 9–11 learn how people protect endangered species by matching the right strategy to a specific threat — protected areas (national parks, marine reserves), captive breeding and reintroduction, anti-poaching patrols, wildlife corridors linking fragmented habitat, and laws banning trade (e.g. the CITES ivory ban). A central idea is that conservation must protect BOTH habitats AND individual species: breeding animals with nowhere safe to release them fails. Documented recoveries (California condor, Arabian oryx) show conservation can succeed, and learners identify concrete habitat-friendly actions children and families can take.

activities.title: Save-the-species planning scenarios
feedback: If captive breeding alone is chosen, in this scenario the graph shows the population rising then plateauing; prompt: 'The young are being bred — but where would they go? What has to be true about that place?'
When habitat protection is added and the curve climbs, name the mechanism: there is now a protected wild home with enough space, food and safety for released animals to survive.

If a single strategy is applied to a mismatched threat (e.g. a trade ban for a habitat-fragmentation problem), point out that in this case the population stalls and ask which threat that species actually faced.

Reinforce successes using real recoveries: 'The California condor and Arabian oryx were brought back from the brink through captive breeding and release into protected wild areas, plus years of ongoing protection — conservation can work, though the condor still needs careful management.'
activities.rationale: Treating conservation as a decision-and-outcome system lets learners reason about fit between threat and strategy and experience the habitat-AND-species point through a contrast, rather than memorising a list. Running a mismatched or single strategy and seeing it stall targets the 'zoos alone save species' and 'one fix for all' misconceptions. Interactive allocation with a playing-forward recovery graph is one concrete way to make this mechanism visible; a tappable conservation map with recovery-story cards could present the same strategies more passively. Recovery curves here are a simplified teaching model of the principle, not an exact ecological forecast, and do not imply that a single strategy must always fail in reality.

Conservation strategies include protected areas, captive breeding and reintroduction, anti-poaching enforcement, wildlife corridors, and trade bans; the California condor and Arabian oryx were recovered from near-extinction by captive breeding and reintroduction.
Effective conservation requires protecting habitat as well as individual species; international trade in endangered species is regulated under CITES.
learnerActions: Take on the role of a conservation manager for a case species shown with its specific threats — for example poaching, a shrinking range, a population too small to recover on its own, or habitat cut into isolated patches.

Choose interventions from a fixed set — protected reserve, anti-poaching patrol, captive-breeding programme, wildlife corridor, trade ban — spending within a limited budget, so you must prioritise rather than pick everything.
Deliberately try saving a species with captive breeding alone first, then watch a recovery graph play the years forward and observe what happens to the population.
Add habitat protection to the captive-breeding case and re-run, comparing the two recovery curves.
Write down, for each case, which threat you were addressing and why your chosen strategy fits that threat.
activities.intendedInsight: Different threats need different, matched interventions, and species and habitat must be protected together: in this model, captive breeding alone plateaus because there is nowhere safe to release the young, and the wild population recovers once habitat is also protected. Real outcomes depend on the species and its threats.

activities.title: Match the threat to the strategy
feedback: For a threat paired with a mismatched strategy, name the actual threat and ask which intervention directly reduces it.

If 'zoos alone = saved' is chosen, respond: captive breeding is only half the job — there must also be protected wild habitat with space, food and safety to release them into, or the species survives only in captivity.
Where the habitat-and-species link is explained well, affirm the reasoning and connect it to the planning scenarios.
activities.rationale: Matching and short-answer items can check whether learners hold the distinctions and can state the habitat-AND-species principle. A sort can check classification but does not itself elicit the richer explanation, so the written short-answer step is included; this activity checks understanding rather than letting learners experience recovery dynamics, and works best alongside the planning activity rather than replacing it.
sourceClaims: Conservation strategies include protected areas, captive breeding and reintroduction, anti-poaching enforcement, wildlife corridors, and trade bans; the California condor and Arabian oryx were recovered from near-extinction by captive breeding and reintroduction.
Effective conservation requires protecting habitat as well as individual species; international trade in endangered species is regulated under CITES.
learnerActions: Sort a set of threats — poaching, habitat loss, a population too small to recover, habitat broken into isolated patches, international trade in animal parts — and pair each with the intervention that best addresses it (patrols for poaching; trade bans for illegal trade/demand; reserves for habitat loss; captive breeding for tiny populations; corridors for fragmentation).
Match named recovered species to the strategy that saved them (e.g. California condor and Arabian oryx to captive breeding and reintroduction).
Answer a short question on whether rising numbers of a bred animal in zoos means the species is saved, and justify the answer.
Explain in a sentence or two why protecting the habitat and helping the individual species have to happen together.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can distinguish the strategies, link them to the threats they fit, and articulate that captive numbers alone do not equal a saved species.

activities.title: Talk with a conservation ranger
feedback: If a learner says only scientists or governments can help, offer concrete actions — planting for pollinators, reducing waste, supporting reserves — and show how many small actions aggregate into habitat protection.
If a learner dismisses unglamorous species, connect to biodiversity: protecting a habitat saves many species at once, including crucial keystone ones that are not big or famous.
Encourage realistic, specific actions tied to habitat rather than slogans.
activities.rationale: A responsive in-role dialogue can surface the human trade-offs and values of conservation and may make 'you can help' concrete by eliciting a learner's own realistic action, and provides a factual recovery (condor) to discuss. It suits the motivational and civic dimension of the topic; the strategy-to-threat reasoning is better practised through the planning and matching activities. The comparative efficacy of dialogue versus other media here is not established by the sources.
sourceClaims: Making and evaluating claims about solutions to problems caused by environmental change; conservation applies science-in-society aims.

Conservation strategies include protected areas, captive breeding and reintroduction, anti-poaching enforcement, wildlife corridors, and trade bans; the California condor and Arabian oryx were recovered from near-extinction by captive breeding and reintroduction.
learnerActions: Discuss in role with a conservation scientist or park ranger who describes a real recovery such as the California condor, including the hard choices and trade-offs behind it (funding limits, community needs, deciding what to prioritise).
Ask and answer questions about why a single success story still required years of effort and a protected place to return animals to.
Respond to the prompt: 'What is one thing you or your family could do that would genuinely help wildlife?' and explain how many small habitat-friendly actions add up.
activities.intendedInsight: Real conservation involves trade-offs, funding and community values voiced by people, and ordinary individuals and families can contribute through concrete habitat-friendly choices.

constraints: Cover at least three strategies with real success stories, and make the habitat-AND-species point explicit using a counter-case (breeding with nowhere to release fails).
Include realistic, specific child/family actions tied to habitat so 'you can help' is concrete, not a platitude.
Frame conservation as matching the right strategy to the specific threat, so learners reason about fit rather than only listing actions.
Use documented recoveries (condor, oryx) to build agency rather than despair, while being honest that recovery took sustained effort and protected habitat.

Matching and multiple-choice items check recognition of the ideas and can catch common misconceptions; on their own they do not let a learner experience recovery dynamics or construct a plan, so pair them with the planning activity.

A tappable conservation map presents strategies and stories but does not require the learner to choose and test a strategy against a threat; treat it as a presentation scaffold, not the core decision-making task.

The recovery-graph outcomes are simplified models of real population dynamics; present them as illustrative of the principle, not as precise ecological predictions for any specific species, and do not imply that a single strategy must always fail or a combined one must always succeed in reality.

Checkpoints: at the concrete level a learner names at least one strategy and an animal it helped; at the transitional level they describe three strategies with examples and one action a child can take; at the formal level they match a strategy to the threat it addresses and explain why protecting habitat and species together matters.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; all listed sources carry verified:false in the source row and were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source row rated 3D interactive as adding 'no conceptual value' and framed the quiz as testing 'rather than' teaching. These are catalog fit judgements, not established pedagogical laws; they have been softened to scoped observations about affordances and omitted as universal claims.

Recovery-curve outcomes in any simulation depend on modelling assumptions; reviewers should ensure the 'captive breeding alone plateaus until habitat is protected' behaviour is presented as a principle-illustrating model rather than an exact forecast or a claim that single strategies always fail.
The comparative effectiveness of the conversation, map and planning-sim media is not established by the sources; efficacy wording is kept conditional (can/may/intended).

The specific set of threats, strategies and species examples (condor, oryx, CITES ivory ban) derives from unverified conservation-biology and IUCN/CITES references cited in the row; confirm these case details against current sources before classroom use.

probeDeeper: Once the zoo tigers are ready, where would they go? What has to be true about that place?
Why might protecting a whole rainforest save more species than a programme for just one animal?
Name a real animal that conservation brought back from near-extinction, and say how it was done.
What is one thing you or your family could do that would genuinely help wildlife?
assess.correctAnswer: Breeding in captivity helps, but it isn't enough on its own. To truly save the species the tigers need a protected wild habitat to return to — forest with enough prey and space, kept safe from poaching and destruction. Without protected habitat the animals have nowhere to live wild, and the species survives only in cages. Real conservation protects habitats AND helps individual species (captive breeding, anti-poaching patrols, wildlife corridors, laws) together.

errorPatterns.pattern: Breeding animals in zoos (or just raising the numbers) is enough to save a species
errorPatterns.nextMove: Stress the need for a wild home to return to — captive animals need protected habitat or they only ever survive in cages.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — once the zoo has bred plenty of tigers, the species is saved.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Declares the species saved once zoo numbers rise, with no mention of habitat.

errorPatterns.pattern: Conservation just means stopping people hunting the animal
errorPatterns.nextMove: Survey the range of strategies — reserves, corridors, captive breeding, anti-poaching, laws — and match each to a different threat.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names only hunting bans; omits habitat protection, corridors and invasive control.

errorPatterns.pattern: Only big, cute or famous animals are worth protecting
errorPatterns.nextMove: Connect to biodiversity — protecting a habitat saves many species at once, including unglamorous but crucial keystone ones.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Cares about pandas or tigers but dismisses insects, plants or habitat.

errorPatterns.pattern: Ordinary people and children can't do anything that matters
errorPatterns.nextMove: Give concrete habitat-friendly actions (planting for pollinators, reducing waste, supporting reserves) and show how many small actions add up.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says only scientists or governments can help.

responseLevels.gap: Equates conservation with zoos and breeding, or with only banning hunting; thinks rising captive numbers mean a species is saved and that individuals can't help.
responseLevels.full: Describes multiple strategies with examples (reserves, captive breeding, corridors, anti-poaching, laws), names a species brought back from the brink, explains that conservation needs both habitat protection and species-specific help, and suggests a realistic action people can take.
responseLevels.partial: Lists several strategies and an example, but treats them as separate fixes — doesn't see that saving a species needs BOTH protected habitat AND species-level help, or defaults to captive breeding as the whole answer.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A zoo successfully breeds lots of a rare tiger in its enclosures. A student says: 'Great — now the tiger is saved.' Is breeding them in the zoo enough to save the species? What else is needed?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks numbers-in-captivity equals saved says yes. A child who understands says captive breeding is only half the job — you also need protected wild habitat to release them into. Naming the habitat requirement is the discriminator.
